lessons.title: Muscle Structure and Composition of Meat
lessons.body:
Muscle is about 75% water, 20% protein, and 5% fat and other substances. In butchery, understanding this helps you handle meat properly. When an animal is alive, muscles contract to move. After slaughter, muscles still contain energy (glycogen) that converts to lactic acid, which affects pH and tenderness. A typical beef carcass has a pH of about 5.6 to 5.8 after 24 hours. If the animal was stressed before slaughter, glycogen is depleted, leading to dark, firm, dry (DFD) meat with high pH (above 6.0), which spoils faster. Pale, soft, exudative (PSE) meat occurs in pigs stressed right before slaughter, with low pH and poor water-holding capacity.

Muscle fibers are bundled together by connective tissue. The main proteins are myofibrillar (actin and myosin) and connective tissue (collagen and elastin). Collagen softens with slow, moist cooking, while elastin (in older animals) remains tough. In Africa, many animals are pasture-raised and older, so collagen is stronger. For tough cuts like shank or neck, use slow cooking with moistureâlike a stew or pot roastâto break down collagen into gelatin.

Fat in meat adds flavor and juiciness. Intramuscular fat (marbling) is desirable. In lean game or zebu cattle, marbling is low, so avoid overcooking. Water content affects weight and price. Meat should be stored at 0-4Â°C to prevent bacterial growth. At room temperature (above 5Â°C), bacteria double every 20 minutes. Always use clean surfaces and wash hands with soap.

Practical tip: When cutting, slice across the grain to shorten muscle fibers. This makes meat more tender. For tough cuts, marinate in acidic ingredients like lemon juice or vinegar (pH 2-3) for 2-4 hours to weaken collagen. In African markets, where refrigeration may be limited, sell meat quickly or preserve by drying, salting, or smoking. Understanding muscle composition helps you choose the right cooking method and cut for each part of the animal.

lessons.title: Skeletal Anatomy of Beef, Pork, and Lamb
lessons.body:
Knowing the skeleton helps you break down a carcass efficiently and identify cuts. Beef, pork, and lamb have similar bone structures but differ in size and shape. The spine runs from neck to tail, with cervical (neck), thoracic (rib), lumbar (loin), and sacral (rump) vertebrae. Ribs attach to the thoracic vertebrae. The sternum is the breastbone. The pelvis supports the hind legs. Key bones for butchery: femur (thigh), tibia (shank), humerus (arm), radius/ulna (forearm), and scapula (shoulder blade).

In beef, the carcass is split into quarters: forequarter and hindquarter. The forequarter includes chuck, rib, brisket, shank, and plate. The hindquarter includes loin, round, flank, and shank. Pork is divided into primal cuts: shoulder (Boston butt and picnic), loin, belly, and ham. Lamb is smaller; primal cuts are shoulder, rack, loin, and leg. In Africa, many butchers use a saw or cleaver to cut through bone. A bone saw with 10-14 teeth per inch is ideal for clean cuts.

When breaking down a carcass, follow the seams between muscles. For example, the seam between the rib and loin is at the 5th rib. Use a sharp boning knife (6-inch curved blade) to separate. For pork, the shoulder contains the blade bone and arm bone; remove them for boneless roasts. Lamb racks have 7-8 ribs; French-trim by scraping the bones clean.

Locate the aitchbone (pelvis) in the hindquarter. Cutting through the aitchbone separates the leg from the loin. In beef, the femur is large; use a saw to split the round. In pork, the ham bone (femur) is removed for whole hams. Always cut away from your body and keep knives sharp. In many African settings, carcasses are butchered on a clean table or hanging rail. If no rail, use a sturdy table and sanitize with bleach solution (1 tablespoon per gallon of water).

Practice identifying bones by feel. A beef neck has cervical vertebrae with prominent spines. Pork ribs are flatter than beef ribs. Lamb bones are smaller and softer. Knowing anatomy reduces waste and increases yield. For example, a skilled butcher can get 75-80% yield from a beef carcass, while an inexperienced one may get only 60%. That difference is profit.

lessons.title: Identifying Major Muscles and Their Uses
lessons.body:
Each muscle has a unique texture, fat content, and best use. Learning them helps you sell the right cut for the right dish. Start with the major muscles in beef: ribeye (eye of rib), tenderloin (psoas major), strip loin (longissimus dorsi), sirloin (gluteus medius), top round (semimembranosus), bottom round (biceps femoris), chuck (shoulder clod), brisket (pectoralis), and shank (flexor muscles). Pork: loin (longissimus), tenderloin, Boston butt (shoulder), picnic shoulder, ham (semimembranosus), and belly. Lamb: rack (ribeye), loin, leg (sirloin and round), and shoulder.

Tenderloin is the most tender muscle because it does little work. It runs along the spine inside the loin. In beef, it's the filet mignon. Cook it quickly with high heatâgrill or pan-sear to medium-rare (55-60Â°C internal). In Africa, tenderloin is often sold as a premium cut. Strip loin is also tender; cut into steaks. Ribeye has more fat and flavor; great for grilling. Sirloin is moderately tender; good for roasts or steaks.

Muscles from the leg and shoulder do more work, so they are tougher. Top round (inside round) is lean and tough; use for roasts or slice thin for stir-fry. Bottom round (outside round) is tougher; best for slow cooking or ground meat. Chuck has a lot of connective tissue; perfect for stews or ground beef. Brisket is tough but flavorful; smoke or braise for 4-6 hours. Shank is full of collagen; use for soups and stews.

In pork, the loin is tender; cut into chops. Boston butt is well-marbled; ideal for pulled pork. Ham is lean; cure or roast. Belly is fatty; make bacon. Lamb: rack is tender; grill or roast. Leg is lean and tender; roast whole or cut into steaks. Shoulder is tougher; slow cook for curries.

In African markets, you may not have all these cuts labeled. Teach customers: For tough cuts, use moist heat (boiling, stewing). For tender cuts, use dry heat (grilling, frying). A simple rule: the closer to the spine and the less the muscle moves, the more tender. Use a meat thermometer to check doneness: beef medium-rare 55Â°C, pork 63Â°C, lamb 60Â°C. Always rest meat for 5-10 minutes after cooking to retain juices.

lessons.title: The Science of Rigor Mortis and Aging
lessons.body:
After slaughter, muscles go through rigor mortisâstiffening due to chemical changes. Within 2-6 hours, ATP (energy) depletes, and actin and myosin lock together. The carcass becomes stiff. If you cut meat during rigor, it will be tough. Rigor resolves in 24-48 hours as enzymes break down the lock. In African conditions, if the carcass is not cooled, rigor may pass quickly but bacteria grow fast. Ideal: chill carcass to 0-4Â°C within 1-2 hours after slaughter. If no refrigeration, butcher immediately and cook or preserve.

Aging is holding meat after rigor to improve tenderness and flavor. Two types: wet aging (vacuum-sealed) and dry aging (hanging in controlled environment). Wet aging is common in Africa where vacuum sealers are available. Age beef for 7-14 days at 0-2Â°C. Pork and lamb are usually not aged long; 2-5 days is enough. Dry aging requires 80-85% humidity, 0-2Â°C, and airflow. It concentrates flavor and creates a crust (pellicle) that must be trimmed. Dry aging for 21-45 days gives a nutty, beefy flavor. But it's costly due to weight loss (10-15%) and trim loss.

During aging, enzymes (calpains and cathepsins) break down proteins, increasing tenderness. Flavor develops from fat oxidation and amino acid breakdown. However, aging too long (over 60 days) can cause rancidity. In warm climates, aging without refrigeration is dangerous. If you lack cooling, age for only 1-2 days in a cool, clean room, then sell or freeze.

Practical steps: After slaughter, chill carcass rapidly. For wet aging, cut into primal cuts, vacuum seal, and store at 0-2Â°C. For dry aging, hang whole or primal cuts in a clean cooler with fan. Monitor temperature and humidity daily. Use a calibrated thermometer. If you see slime or smell off odors, discard. In many African butcheries, aging is not practiced due to lack of facilities. Instead, sell fresh meat. But if you can age, you can charge premium prices. For beef, 14-day wet-aged steaks are noticeably more tender than 2-day. Test by cooking a small piece: aged meat is softer and juicier.

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Meat Quality and Palatability
lessons.body:
Meat quality depends on genetics, diet, age, stress, and handling. Palatability includes tenderness, juiciness, and flavor. Breed matters: Bos indicus (zebu) cattle have tougher meat than Bos taurus due to calpastatin enzyme. In Africa, many cattle are zebu; they need longer aging or marinating. Diet: grass-fed meat is leaner and has more omega-3, but less marbling; grain-fed has more marbling and tenderness. Age: older animals have tougher meat and stronger flavor. Slaughter age: beef 18-24 months, pork 5-6 months, lamb 4-6 months for best quality.

Stress before slaughter is critical. Stressed animals produce dark, firm, dry (DFD) meat if glycogen is depleted, or pale, soft, exudative (PSE) meat if acute stress. DFD meat has high pH (>6.0), spoils faster, and has poor flavor. PSE meat is pale, watery, and loses moisture. To avoid: handle animals calmly, provide water, and rest them 12-24 hours before slaughter. In African abattoirs, lairage (holding pen) should be clean and quiet.

Post-slaughter handling: rapid chilling prevents bacterial growth. Meat should be cooled to 0-4Â°C within 24 hours. If chilled too fast (below 0Â°C), cold shortening occurs, making meat tough. If chilled too slow, bacteria multiply. Use a thermometer. Electrical stimulation (low voltage, 20-50V) can improve tenderness by accelerating rigor. But not common in small African butcheries.

Cooking method affects palatability. Tender cuts: dry heat (grilling, roasting) to medium-rare. Tough cuts: moist heat (braising, stewing) for 2-4 hours. Marinating with acid (lemon, vinegar, papaya) or salt (brine) can improve tenderness. Salt (2-3% solution) for 12-24 hours increases water retention. In Africa, traditional methods like pounding meat with a wooden mallet or using papaya leaves (containing papain) are effective. Always rest cooked meat before slicing to retain juices. Use a sharp knife to cut across the grain. Serve at 60-65Â°C for best flavor.

lessons.title: Introduction to Meat Grading and Inspection
lessons.body:
Grading and inspection ensure meat safety and quality. Inspection is mandatory for wholesomeness; grading is voluntary for quality. In Africa, many countries have meat inspection services, but enforcement varies. Inspection looks for diseases (tuberculosis, brucellosis, cysticercosis) and contamination. Ante-mortem (before slaughter) and post-mortem (after) inspections are done by trained inspectors. Look for signs: fever, abscesses, parasites, abnormal color or smell. If found, condemn the carcass. In small butcheries, you must self-inspect: check lymph nodes (enlarged = disease), liver (spots = flukes), lungs (pneumonia), and intestines (parasites).

Grading evaluates quality: marbling, maturity, color, texture. In beef, USDA grades (Prime, Choice, Select) are common but not universal in Africa. Many countries use their own systems. For example, South Africa uses A1, A2, A3 based on age and fat. A1 is young, lean; A3 is older, fatter. In East Africa, grading is less formal. You can grade manually: Prime (abundant marbling, young), Choice (moderate marbling), Select (slight marbling), Standard (minimal marbling). Pork grades: 1, 2, 3, 4 based on backfat and muscling. Lamb: Prime, Choice, Good.

Inspection also covers hygiene: slaughterhouse cleanliness, water quality, worker health. Use potable water. Wear clean aprons, boots, and hairnets. Sterilize knives in 82Â°C water. Clean tables with 200 ppm chlorine solution. In many African markets, meat is sold on wooden tables; switch to plastic or stainless steel for easy cleaning. Cover meat to prevent flies. Keep offal separate from muscle meat.

Grading helps pricing. Prime cuts sell for 30-50% more than Select. Teach customers to identify quality: firm, dry surface, bright red color (beef), pink (pork), light red (lamb). Avoid meat that is slimy, dark, or has off odor. For your business, develop a simple grading system: Grade A (best), Grade B (good), Grade C (economy). Label clearly. This builds trust. In Kenya, butchers who grade meat often get repeat customers. Always keep records of inspection and grading. If you sell uninspected meat, you risk fines and illness. When in doubt, cook meat thoroughly to 71Â°C to kill bacteria.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Meat Science and Animal Anatomy for Butchery

In African butchery businesses, the difference between profit and loss is often decided before the knife touches the carcass. Understanding muscle structure, skeletal anatomy, rigor mortis, aging, and meat grading allows butchers to buy smarter, cut more accurately, reduce waste, and price products correctly. This practical reference module brings together the core science from the six lessons in this course and translates it into daily decisions for butcheries operating in formal and informal markets across Africa.

Whether you are supplying high-end restaurants in Nairobi, running a busy township butchery in Johannesburg, or trading in a municipal market in Accra, the same biological principles apply. Meat is a perishable, high-value product. Every hour of delay, every degree of temperature rise, and every incorrect cut destroys margin. This reference is designed to be used at the block, at the display counter, and at the buying point.

1. Muscle Structure and Composition: What You Are Actually Selling

Meat is composed of water (approximately 70â75%), protein (15â20%), fat (2â15% depending on species and cut), and small amounts of minerals and carbohydrates. Muscle tissue consists of bundles of muscle fibres held together by connective tissue. The amount and type of connective tissue determines tenderness. Collagen, found in tendons and silverskin, is tough and requires slow, moist cooking to break down. Elastin, found in ligaments and neck muscles, does not soften with heat and must be removed by the butcher.

For the butcher, this means that cuts from heavily exercised musclesâneck, shank, and legâcontain more connective tissue and should be sold as stewing, braising, or mincing meat. Cuts from less-exercised musclesâloin and ribâare naturally tender and command premium prices as grilling or roasting cuts. Understanding this allows you to allocate each carcass part to its highest-value use, maximising revenue per animal.

2. Skeletal Anatomy of Beef, Pork, and Lamb

The skeleton provides the framework for all cuts. In beef, the vertebral column runs from the neck (cervical) through the thoracic (rib) region to the lumbar (loin) and sacral (rump) regions. The number and size of vertebrae determine the length of the loin and rib sections, which are the highest-value primals. In pork, the skeleton is similar but smaller, with a proportionally longer loin and a distinctive shoulder structure. Lamb has a lighter frame with a higher ratio of bone to meat, meaning yield percentages are lower and pricing must account for this.

Knowing the skeleton helps you locate joints, separate primals cleanly, and avoid bone fragments in retail cuts. It also helps you estimate carcass yield: beef typically yields 55â65% of live weight as carcass, pork 70â75%, and lamb 45â55%. These figures directly affect your buying price per kilogram of saleable meat.

Table 1: Typical Carcass Yield and Composition by Species
Species Dressing % (carcass/live weight) Saleable Meat % of Carcass Bone % of Carcass Fat % of Carcass
Beef55â65%65â72%15â20%10â18%
Pork70â75%68â75%12â16%12â20%
Lamb45â55%60â68%18â24%10â18%

Source: FAO, Manual on Meat Inspection for Developing Countries (FAO Animal Production and Health Paper 119, 1994), Table 2.1, p. 18. Available at fao.org.

3. Identifying Major Muscles and Their Uses

Each muscle has a specific function in the live animal, and that function determines its eating quality. The longissimus dorsi (ribeye and loin) is the premium grilling cut in all species. The psoas major (fillet/tenderloin) is the most tender muscle because it does almost no work. The semimembranosus and biceps femoris (topside and silverside) are lean but less tender, ideal for roasting or slicing. The masseter (cheek) and diaphragm (skirt) are highly flavoured but tough, best for slow cooking or mincing.

In African markets, where customers often buy specific cuts for traditional dishesâsuch as nyama choma in East Africa, braai in Southern Africa, or suya in West Africaâknowing muscle function allows you to recommend the right cut for the right dish. This builds customer trust and reduces returns.

Table 2: Major Muscles, Their Location, and Best Uses
Muscle Location Tenderness Best Use
Longissimus dorsiRib and loinHighGrilling, roasting, nyama choma
Psoas majorLoin (inner)Very highFillet, pan-frying, premium grilling
SemimembranosusTopside (hind leg)MediumRoasting, slicing, biltong
Biceps femorisSilverside (hind leg)Medium-lowSlow roasting, corned beef, mincing
MasseterCheekLowSlow cooking, stewing, mincing
DiaphragmSkirt / flankLowSlow cooking, braising, mincing

Source: Adapted from FAO, Guidelines for Slaughtering, Meat Cutting and Further Processing (1991), Table 3, pp. 22â24; and Lawrie, R.A. & Ledward, D.A., Lawrie's Meat Science, 7th ed. (Woodhead Publishing, 2006), Chapter 4.

4. The Science of Rigor Mortis and Aging

After slaughter, muscle glycogen converts to lactic acid, causing pH to fall from about 7.0 to 5.5â5.8. This triggers rigor mortisâthe stiffening of muscles as actin and myosin filaments lock together. Rigor begins 2â6 hours post-slaughter and resolves in 12â24 hours for beef, 4â8 hours for pork, and 6â12 hours for lamb. If meat is cut before rigor resolves, it will be tough and dry. If it is chilled too rapidly before rigor, cold shortening occurs, also causing toughness.

Aging (conditioning) is the controlled storage of meat after rigor to allow natural enzymes to break down connective tissue and improve tenderness and flavour. Beef is typically aged 7â21 days; lamb 5â10 days; pork is usually not aged beyond 2â3 days because it is lean and prone to spoilage. In Africa, where cold chain infrastructure may be limited, dry aging in a controlled room or vacuum-packed wet aging is recommended. Proper aging can increase the value of beef by 15â30% in premium markets.

â  SAFETY WARNING: Temperature and Time Control

Meat must be kept below 5Â°C during storage and transport. Between 5Â°C and 60Â°C, bacteria such as Salmonella, E. coli, and Listeria multiply rapidly. In many African markets, cold chain failures are the leading cause of meat spoilage and foodborne illness. Never leave carcasses or cuts at ambient temperature for more than 2 hours. If you cannot maintain the cold chain, process and sell meat within the same day, and use ice or cool boxes for transport. Always wash hands, knives, and surfaces with clean water and disinfectant between handling different species and cuts. Sick or injured animals must never enter the food chain without veterinary inspection.

5. Factors Affecting Meat Quality and Palatability

Meat quality is determined by breed, age, sex, diet, stress at slaughter, and post-slaughter handling. Stress before slaughter depletes glycogen, leading to dark, firm, dry (DFD) meat with high pH and poor keeping quality. Conversely, acute stress can cause pale, soft, exudative (PSE) meat, especially in pork. In African contexts, where animals may be transported long distances on poor roads, stress is a major quality risk. Buying from local, well-managed farms reduces this risk.

Palatability has three components: tenderness, juiciness, and flavour. Tenderness is influenced by connective tissue, muscle fibre type, and aging. Juiciness depends on intramuscular fat (marbling) and water-holding capacity. Flavour is affected by diet (grass-fed vs grain-fed), breed, and cooking method. For butchers, understanding these factors helps in selecting suppliers, grading carcasses, and advising customers on cooking methods.

6. Introduction to Meat Grading and Inspection

Grading classifies meat by quality (marbling, maturity, colour, texture) and yield (ratio of lean to fat and bone). In Africa, formal grading systems vary by country. South Africa uses the SA Meat Classification System (A1, A2, A3, etc.), while Kenya and Nigeria rely more on visual inspection and weight. Inspection, by contrast, is mandatory and focuses on safetyâdetecting disease, contamination, and spoilage. Always buy inspected meat and keep records of your suppliers.

For your business, grading allows you to price cuts accurately and target different customer segments. A well-marbled A2 beef ribeye can be sold at a premium to restaurants, while A3 or older animal cuts can be minced or sold for stewing. Knowing the difference protects your margin and your reputation.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Verify that all meat comes from inspected and approved slaughter facilities.
  • â Check pH or rigor status before cuttingânever cut pre-rigor meat for retail.
  • â Age beef 7â21 days, lamb 5â10 days, and pork no more than 2â3 days.
  • â Keep all meat below 5Â°C from slaughter to sale; use ice or cool boxes in transport.
  • â Identify muscles correctly and allocate each to its highest-value use.
  • â Remove all elastin (ligaments) and excess collagen (silverskin) before display.
  • â Record supplier, date, species, and grade for every carcass received.
  • â Train staff on hygiene, knife safety, and cold chain management every quarter.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Guidelines for Slaughtering, Meat Cutting and Further Processing (free full text)
  • FAO â Manual on Meat Inspection for Developing Countries (free full text)
  • FAO â Meat Processing Technology for Small- to Medium-Scale Producers (PDF)
  • USDA Agricultural Research Service â Meat Science Research (free resources)
  • WOAH (OIE) â Terrestrial Animal Health Code: Meat Inspection Standards (free access)

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills Butchery course. For business-first training, pair this reference with costing sheets, supplier contracts, and customer cut guides specific to your market.

quiz.q: What is the approximate water content of muscle?
quiz.explanation: Muscle is about 75% water, which affects weight and juiciness.

quiz.q: What condition results from stress right before slaughter in pigs?
quiz.explanation: PSE (pale, soft, exudative) occurs due to acute stress and rapid pH drop.

quiz.q: Which protein softens with slow, moist cooking?
quiz.explanation: Collagen breaks down into gelatin when cooked with moisture and low heat.

quiz.q: What is the ideal storage temperature for fresh meat?
quiz.explanation: 0-4Â°C slows bacterial growth without freezing.

quiz.q: Which bone is part of the hindquarter?
quiz.explanation: The femur is the thigh bone in the hindquarter.

quiz.q: How many ribs are typically in a lamb rack?
quiz.explanation: A lamb rack usually has 7-8 ribs.

quiz.q: What is the best tool for cutting through bone?
quiz.explanation: A bone saw with 10-14 teeth per inch makes clean cuts through bone.

quiz.q: Which muscle is the most tender?
quiz.explanation: Tenderloin does little work, so it is the most tender muscle.

quiz.q: What cooking method is best for top round?
quiz.explanation: Top round is lean and tough; slow moist cooking makes it tender.

quiz.q: What is the internal temperature for medium-rare beef?
quiz.explanation: Medium-rare beef is cooked to 55Â°C.

quiz.q: What causes rigor mortis?
quiz.explanation: Rigor mortis occurs when ATP is depleted and actin-myosin lock.

quiz.q: How long does rigor mortis typically last?
quiz.explanation: Rigor resolves in 24-48 hours as enzymes break down the lock.

quiz.q: What is wet aging?
quiz.explanation: Wet aging is storing meat in vacuum-sealed bags at 0-2Â°C.

quiz.q: What is the ideal aging time for beef wet aging?
quiz.explanation: 7-14 days of wet aging improves tenderness without excessive cost.

quiz.q: What is the pellicle in dry aging?
quiz.explanation: The pellicle is a dried crust that forms on the surface and must be trimmed.

quiz.q: Which breed of cattle generally has tougher meat?
quiz.explanation: Bos indicus (zebu) cattle have higher calpastatin, making meat tougher.

quiz.q: What is DFD meat?
quiz.explanation: DFD stands for dark, firm, dry, caused by chronic stress before slaughter.

quiz.q: What is the recommended lairage time before slaughter?
quiz.explanation: Resting animals 12-24 hours reduces stress and improves meat quality.

quiz.q: What is cold shortening?
quiz.explanation: Cold shortening occurs when meat is chilled too fast, causing toughness.

quiz.q: Which marinade ingredient can tenderize meat?
quiz.explanation: Papaya contains papain, an enzyme that breaks down protein.

quiz.q: What does meat inspection look for?
quiz.explanation: Inspection ensures wholesomeness by checking for diseases and contamination.

quiz.q: What is a sign of disease in lymph nodes?
quiz.explanation: Enlarged lymph nodes can indicate infection or disease.

quiz.q: What does USDA Prime grade indicate?
quiz.explanation: Prime has the most marbling and is highest quality.

quiz.q: What is the chlorine concentration for sanitizing meat tables?
quiz.explanation: 200 ppm chlorine solution is effective for sanitizing surfaces.

quiz.q: What temperature should knives be sterilized at?
quiz.explanation: Sterilize knives in water at 82Â°C to kill bacteria.

quiz.q: What is a simple grading system for a small butchery?
quiz.explanation: Any clear grading system can be used; consistency builds trust.

quiz.q: What is the safe internal temperature for cooking meat to kill bacteria?
quiz.explanation: 71Â°C kills most bacteria, ensuring safety.

quiz.q: Which muscle is used for pulled pork?
quiz.explanation: Boston butt is well-marbled and ideal for slow cooking and pulling.

quiz.q: What is the pH of normal beef after 24 hours?
quiz.explanation: Normal beef pH is 5.6-5.8 after rigor resolution.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of aging meat?
quiz.explanation: Aging uses enzymes to break down proteins, improving tenderness and flavor.
